question:
Select the word segment that substitutes (replaces) the bracketed word segment correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully. Select the option 'no correction required' if the sentence is correct as given.

He gritted his teeth and tried to act as though he (either noticed nor cared).
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. neither noticed nor cared.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Either" is always paired with or, and "neither" is always paired with nor. Mixing them ("either…nor") is a fixed-pair error. (सहसंबंधी समुच्चयबोधक — correlative conjunctions)

◦ The sense of the sentence is negative — he pretended he did not notice and did not care — so the negative pair neither…nor is required.

◦ Correct: He gritted his teeth and tried to act as though he neither noticed nor cared.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is wrong because the printed segment "either noticed nor cared" is an incorrect pairing and does need correction.

• Option 3 "either noticed or cared" is grammatically valid but reverses the meaning into a positive/alternative sense, which does not fit "gritted his teeth".

• Option 4 "neither noticed cared" drops "nor" altogether, leaving the pair incomplete.

NOTE

• Common correlative pairs: either…or, neither…nor, both…and, not only…but also, whether…or, no sooner…than, hardly…when, scarcely…when.

• With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject: "Neither the boys nor the teacher was present."

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Her ribs were ______ but no longer painful.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. sore.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sore (adjective) means painful or tender to the touch, especially after injury or strain. (दर्द भरा / पीड़ादायक)

◦ The contrast marker "but no longer painful" shows the blank needs an adjective describing lingering tenderness, and only "sore" is such an adjective.

◦ Correct: Her ribs were sore but no longer painful.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "soar" is a verb meaning to fly or rise high (उड़ान भरना) — a verb cannot follow "were" here as a description of ribs.

• Option 3 "sour" means acidic or bitter in taste (खट्टा) and is not used for bodily pain.

• Option 4 "sure" means certain (निश्चित) and makes no sense with "ribs".

NOTE

• Homophone set to remember: soar (to fly high) / sore (painful) / sour (acidic).

• Useful collocations: a sore throat, a sore point, sore eyes; prices soar, spirits soar.

question:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.

Harry's eyes watered in / the chill as they soar upwards; he / could see nothing below now.
option_2: the chill as they soar upwards; he
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. the chill as they soar upwards; he.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence is narrated in the past tense ("watered", "could see"), so the verb in the subordinate clause must also be in the past tense — soared, not "soar". (काल की एकरूपता — sequence/consistency of tenses)

◦ The rule of the sequence of tenses says that when the principal clause is in the past, the subordinate clause normally takes a past form.

◦ Correct: Harry's eyes watered in the chill as they soared upwards; he could see nothing below now.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "could see nothing below now" is correct — "could" is the past form of "can" and matches the narration.

• Option 3 "Harry's eyes watered in" is correct — the possessive apostrophe and the past verb "watered" are both fine.

• Option 4 "No error" is wrong because the segment in Option 2 does contain a tense error.

NOTE

• Exception to the rule: a universal truth stays in the present even after a past main verb — "The teacher said that the earth revolves round the sun."

• Watch for such SSC error-spotting traps: subject-verb agreement, tense shift, wrong preposition, and misuse of articles.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.

A health person may carry germs of typhoid, cholera, dysentery, etc. in his body.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. healthy person may.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A noun must be modified by an adjective, not by another noun of state. "Health" is a noun; the adjective form is healthy. (स्वस्थ — healthy)

◦ The article "A" before the blank demands a singular noun, so "person" (not "persons") must be retained.

◦ "May" correctly expresses possibility, which suits a general statement about carrying germs.

◦ Correct: A healthy person may carry germs of typhoid, cholera, dysentery, etc. in his body.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "health persons might" keeps the noun "health" as a modifier and wrongly uses the plural "persons" after "A".

• Option 3 "No improvement" is wrong because "health person" is ungrammatical.

• Option 4 "healthy persons would" breaks singular-plural agreement with "A", and "would" wrongly suggests a condition rather than possibility.

NOTE

• Noun → adjective pairs frequently tested: health – healthy, wealth – wealthy, danger – dangerous, courage – courageous, beauty – beautiful.

• May = possibility/permission; might = weaker/remoter possibility; would = past of "will" or a conditional.

question:
Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word.

Similar
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Unlike.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Similar means alike, resembling one another. (समान / एक जैसा)

◦ Unlike means different from, not resembling — the exact antonym of "similar". (भिन्न / असमान)

◦ Correct: Her handwriting is quite unlike her brother's, though people expect them to be similar.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Bizarre" means strange or very odd (विचित्र) — it is not the opposite of "similar".

• Option 2 "Resemblant" means resembling or alike, which is a synonym, not an antonym.

• Option 4 "Secretive" means inclined to keep things hidden (गुप्त स्वभाव का) and is unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• Synonyms of *similar*: alike, analogous, comparable, akin, identical, parallel.

• Antonyms of *similar*: unlike, dissimilar, different, divergent, disparate, contrasting.

question:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.

Hearing those words / from his mouth, was / hard than I thought.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. hard than I thought.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The conjunction than signals a comparison, and a comparison requires the comparative degree of the adjective — "harder", not the positive form "hard". (तुलनात्मक अवस्था)

◦ One-syllable adjectives form the comparative by adding -er: hard → harder.

◦ Correct: Hearing those words from his mouth was harder than I thought.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "No error" is wrong because the degree of comparison is faulty in the last segment.

• Option 3 "Hearing those words" is correct — the gerund phrase functions properly as the subject.

• Option 4 "from his mouth, was" is correct — the singular verb "was" agrees with the gerund subject "Hearing".

NOTE

• Degree rules: positive + as…as; comparative + than; superlative + the and often of/in all.

• Never use a double comparative: "more harder", "more better" are wrong. Also remember Latin comparatives take to, not "than": superior to, inferior to, senior to, prefer to.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom

To pull your weight
option_1: To do your full share of work
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. To do your full share of work.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom to pull your weight means to do your fair and full share of the work in a joint task. (अपने हिस्से का पूरा काम करना)

◦ It comes from rowing, where every member of the crew must pull the oar in proportion to his weight for the boat to move well.

◦ Correct: If everyone in the team pulls their weight, we will finish the project on time.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "To help one's relatives" describes nepotism/favouritism, not this idiom.

• Option 3 "To buy something" is a literal act and has no link with the idiom's sense of shared effort.

• Option 4 "To give something" is again a literal meaning and does not convey doing one's share of labour.

NOTE

• Related work idioms: to burn the midnight oil (to work late into the night), to put one's shoulder to the wheel (to work hard), to pass the buck (to shift responsibility), to shirk work (to avoid duty).

• Opposite in spirit: to sit on the fence, to twiddle one's thumbs (to remain idle).

question:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.

At night, lying sleepless, he considered / sending messengers besides the country, / secretly, in search of his friend.
option_1: secretly, in search of his friend.
option_2: At night, lying sleepless, he considered
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. sending messengers besides the country,

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Besides means "in addition to / apart from", whereas the sentence needs a preposition of place expressing movement out of the country — beyond (or "across"). (के अतिरिक्त बनाम परे)

◦ Messengers are being sent out beyond the borders of the country to look for his friend, so "besides" is the wrong preposition here.

◦ Correct: At night, lying sleepless, he considered sending messengers beyond the country, secretly, in search of his friend.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "secretly, in search of his friend" is correct — "in search of" is the standard fixed phrase.

• Option 2 "At night, lying sleepless, he considered" is correct — "at night" is the right time preposition and the participle phrase is properly placed.

• Option 4 "No error" is wrong because the preposition in Option 3 is faulty.

NOTE

• Beside = by the side of; besides = in addition to / moreover. "He sat beside me." / "Besides English, she knows French."

• Other confusing prepositions: between (two) vs among (more than two); in (larger places/months/years) vs at (specific points/time).

question: Four words are given, out of which three words are spelt correctly. Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Publically.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is publicly — the adverb of "public" is formed by adding -ly directly to the adjective, with no "-al-" in between. (सार्वजनिक रूप से)

◦ "Public" is the rare adjective ending in -ic whose adverb does not take "-ally"; almost all others do (basic → basically, tragic → tragically).

◦ Correct: The minister publicly apologised for the remark.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Referred" is correctly spelt — the final consonant is doubled because the stress falls on the last syllable (re-FER).

• Option 2 "Recommend" is correctly spelt — one "c", two "m"s.

• Option 3 "Separate" is correctly spelt — remember "there is a rat in sep-a-rat-e".

NOTE

• Frequently misspelt SSC words: occurrence, maintenance, committee, embarrass, privilege, necessary, accommodation, questionnaire.

• Doubling rule: refer → referred, prefer → preferred, but offer → offered and benefit → benefited (stress not on the last syllable).

question:
Select the most appropriate word for the given group of words.

The art of careful public speaking, using clear pronunciation
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Elocution.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Elocution is the skill or art of clear, expressive public speaking, especially with correct pronunciation and articulation. (वाक्पटुता / भाषण-कला)

◦ It comes from the Latin *eloqui* meaning "to speak out", the same root as "eloquent".

◦ Correct: She won the inter-school elocution contest with her flawless delivery.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "Incubation" is the process of hatching eggs, or the period between infection and the appearance of symptoms (ऊष्मायन काल).

• Option 3 "Abdication" is the formal giving up of a throne, power or office (सिंहासन/पद त्याग) — e.g. the abdication of a king.

• Option 4 "Obrution" is not a standard English word and carries no such meaning.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions: Oratory — the art of formal public speaking; Eloquence — fluent, persuasive speech; Soliloquy — speaking one's thoughts aloud when alone; Loquacious — very talkative; Garrulous — talkative about trivial things.

question:
Select the word from the options which is similar in meaning to the bracketed word given in the sentence below.

They are institutions built to hold and (continue) power for a political group.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. maintain.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In this sentence continue means to keep something going without a break — to retain or preserve it. (बनाए रखना)

◦ Maintain carries exactly this sense of keeping power in existence, and it pairs naturally with "hold" in "hold and maintain power".

◦ Correct: They are institutions built to hold and maintain power for a political group.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "abandon" means to give up or desert (छोड़ देना) — the opposite of continuing.

• Option 2 "waste" means to use carelessly or squander (बर्बाद करना) and does not mean to continue.

• Option 4 "release" means to set free or let go (मुक्त करना), again the opposite of retaining power.

NOTE

• Synonyms of *continue/maintain*: sustain, retain, preserve, uphold, perpetuate, prolong.

• Antonyms: abandon, discontinue, cease, relinquish, forsake, surrender.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The ______ term "wasteland" is proposed to be replaced by the term "urban commons."
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. derogatory.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Derogatory means insulting, belittling or showing a critically low opinion of something. (अपमानजनक / निंदात्मक)

◦ The sentence explains that the term "wasteland" is being replaced, which implies the existing term is objectionable — only "derogatory" supplies that negative sense.

◦ Correct: The derogatory term "wasteland" is proposed to be replaced by the term "urban commons."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "lucrative" means profitable or money-making (लाभदायक) and cannot describe a term being rejected.

• Option 3 "imperative" means absolutely necessary or a command (अत्यावश्यक), which does not explain the need for replacement.

• Option 4 "indicative" means serving as a sign of something (सूचक); it is neutral and gives no reason for replacing the word.

NOTE

• Synonyms of *derogatory*: disparaging, demeaning, pejorative, belittling, insulting, uncomplimentary.

• Antonyms: complimentary, flattering, laudatory, appreciative.

question:
Select the word from the options which is exactly opposite in meaning to the bracketed word given in the sentence below.

The Prime Minister is making no (rash) promises.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Considerate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rash means acting or done hastily without thinking of the consequences. (उतावला / अविवेकी)

◦ Considerate means thoughtful and careful about the effect of one's actions on others — the opposite of acting without thought. (विचारशील)

◦ Correct: The Prime Minister is making only considerate, well-thought-out promises rather than rash ones.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "Immature" means childish or not fully developed (अपरिपक्व) — close in spirit to "rash", not opposite.

• Option 3 "Audacious" means daring or recklessly bold (दुस्साहसी), which is a synonym of "rash".

• Option 4 "Bold" means fearless and confident (साहसी) and again leans towards, not away from, "rash".

NOTE

• Synonyms of *rash*: reckless, impulsive, hasty, impetuous, foolhardy, imprudent.

• Antonyms of *rash*: considerate, cautious, prudent, careful, judicious, circumspect.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

Liberty
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Freedom.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Liberty means the state of being free from oppressive restrictions imposed by authority on one's way of life, behaviour or political views. (स्वतंत्रता)

◦ Freedom carries the same meaning and is its closest synonym.

◦ Correct: The Constitution guarantees every citizen the liberty (freedom) of speech and expression.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Statue" is a carved or cast figure (मूर्ति); the link with "Statue of Liberty" is a trap based on association, not meaning.

• Option 3 "Dependence" means relying on someone or something (निर्भरता) — an antonym of liberty.

• Option 4 "Acclamation" means loud and enthusiastic approval (जयघोष / प्रशंसा) and is unrelated.

NOTE

• Synonyms of *liberty*: freedom, independence, autonomy, emancipation, self-determination.

• Antonyms: slavery, bondage, captivity, subjugation, dependence, servitude.

question: Four sentences are given, out of which three have spelling errors. Choose the sentence with all correctly spelt words.
option_2: The teacher told him to watch his grammer.
option_3: My friend happend by around dinnertime.
option_4: That was an impressive and an irresistable necklace.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Thousands protested the election fraud.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Every word in Option 1 — "Thousands", "protested", "election", "fraud" — is spelt correctly, so it is the required sentence. (चुनावी धोखाधड़ी)

◦ The other three sentences each contain one misspelt word, which rules them out.

◦ Correct: Thousands protested the election fraud.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 misspells grammer; the correct spelling is grammar (with "-ar" at the end).

• Option 3 misspells happend; the correct past form is happened.

• Option 4 misspells irresistable; the correct spelling is irresistible (with "-ible").

NOTE

• -ible words: irresistible, possible, edible, visible, responsible, flexible.

• -able words: acceptable, comfortable, remarkable, unbelievable, inevitable.

• Other commonly confused endings: calendar (not calender), grammar (not grammer), stationery (goods) vs stationary (still).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'no substitution required'.

The ban has landed the circus managements a tricky (situation as they can neither use them for the shows or) abandon them.
option_1: situation as they can neither use them for the shows nor
option_2: situation as they cannot either use them for the shows nor
option_4: situation as them can either use them for the shows or
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. situation as they can neither use them for the shows nor.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correlative conjunction neither must always be completed by nor, never by "or". (सहसंबंधी युग्म)

◦ The two things joined must also be parallel — here two bare infinitives after "can": "neither use … nor abandon".

◦ Correct: The ban has landed the circus managements a tricky situation as they can neither use them for the shows nor abandon them.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 pairs "cannot either" with "nor", producing a faulty pairing and a double negative.

• Option 3 "No substitution required" is wrong because the printed "neither … or" is an incorrect pairing.

• Option 4 uses the object pronoun "them" as the subject of "can" (it should be "they") and keeps the wrong "either … or" sense.

NOTE

• Correlatives to memorise: neither…nor, either…or, not only…but also, both…and, whether…or, such…that, so…that.

• Parallelism rule: whatever part of speech follows the first correlative must follow the second — "He is not only intelligent but also hard-working."

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Some were very shaky and unstable, others were ______, and a few were both!
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. convoluted.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Convoluted means extremely complex, twisted and difficult to follow. (उलझा हुआ / जटिल)

◦ The sentence contrasts one defect ("shaky and unstable") with another ("convoluted"), and then says a few had both — so the blank needs a second recognised flaw, which "convoluted" supplies.

◦ Correct: Some were very shaky and unstable, others were convoluted, and a few were both!

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "voluted" merely means having a spiral scroll-like ornament (an architectural term) and is not used to describe arguments or structures being flawed.

• Option 2 "diluted" means weakened by adding water or by reducing strength (पतला किया हुआ) and does not fit the contrast.

• Option 4 "involuted" means curled inwards; it is a rare technical word and is not the standard choice for "complicated".

NOTE

• Synonyms of *convoluted*: complicated, intricate, tangled, labyrinthine, tortuous, byzantine.

• Antonyms: simple, straightforward, clear, lucid, uncomplicated.

question:
The statement below has been given with bracketed text. Select the option with correct idiom for the bracketed text.

They were really (selecting from the last or worst of the resources left) when they picked you.
option_1: scraping the bottom of the barrel
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. scraping the bottom of the barrel.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom to scrape the bottom of the barrel means to be forced to use the last, poorest or least desirable of what is available. (बचे-खुचे या घटिया विकल्पों से काम चलाना)

◦ The image is of scraping out the dregs left at the bottom of a barrel once all the good contents are gone — exactly "the last or worst of the resources left".

◦ Correct: They were really scraping the bottom of the barrel when they picked you.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "rolling the stones" is not a standard idiom; the real proverb is "A rolling stone gathers no moss".

• Option 3 "pulling up snakes" is not an English idiom at all.

• Option 4 "going haywire" means to become badly disordered or to stop working properly, which does not match the given meaning.

NOTE

• Similar idioms: the last straw (the final irritation), a Hobson's choice (no real alternative), beggars can't be choosers (one must accept what is offered).

• Barrel idioms: a barrel of laughs (great fun), have someone over a barrel (to have someone at your mercy).

question:
Select the most appropriate word for the given group of words.

License granted to an individual or group to market a company's goods or services in a particular territory
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Franchise.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A franchise is an authorisation or licence granted by a company to an individual or group to sell its goods or services in a specified area. (अधिकार-पत्र / फ्रेंचाइजी)

◦ The definition mentions a licence, a grantee and a particular territory — the three defining features of a franchise arrangement.

◦ Correct: He bought a fast-food franchise for the whole of eastern Uttar Pradesh.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Branding" is the act of creating a distinctive name, symbol and image for a product (ब्रांडिंग), not a territorial licence.

• Option 2 "Marketing" is the broad activity of promoting and selling products (विपणन) and involves no grant of rights.

• Option 3 "Monopoly" is exclusive control of the supply of a commodity by one seller (एकाधिकार), which is different from a licensed dealership.

NOTE

• "Franchise" also means the right to vote in elections — "universal adult franchise" is guaranteed in India by Article 326 of the Constitution.

• Related business terms: patent (exclusive right to an invention), copyright (right over creative work), trademark (protected brand sign).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

A loud thud woke up everybody and nobody knew what all the ______ was about.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. commotion.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Commotion means a state of confused and noisy disturbance. (हलचल / शोरगुल)

◦ The clue "A loud thud woke up everybody" points to noise and disturbance, so "commotion" is the only word that fits the context.

◦ Correct: A loud thud woke up everybody and nobody knew what all the commotion was about.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "exoneration" means the act of clearing someone of blame (दोषमुक्ति) and has nothing to do with noise.

• Option 3 "abomination" means something that causes disgust or hatred (घृणित वस्तु), which does not suit the context.

• Option 4 "culmination" means the highest or final point of something (चरम बिंदु) and is unrelated to a sudden noise.

NOTE

• Synonyms of *commotion*: uproar, tumult, hubbub, pandemonium, furore, hullabaloo, bedlam.

• Antonyms: calm, quiet, tranquillity, peace, stillness.

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

The term Democracy (1) ______ from the Greek (2) ______ dēmos (people) and Kratos (power). In its (3) ______ meaning, democracy means the "rule of the people". In fact it is a form of government in which all eligible people have an (4) ______ say in the decisions that affect their lives. Democracy (5) ______ a political systems existed in some Greek city-states, notably Athens following a popular uprising in 508 BC.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. comes.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage states a universal/etymological fact, and permanent facts are always expressed in the simple present tense. (सामान्य वर्तमान काल)

◦ The subject "The term Democracy" is singular third person, so the verb takes -s: comes.

◦ Correct: The term Democracy comes from the Greek words dēmos (people) and Kratos (power).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "came" is simple past and wrongly suggests the derivation is no longer true.

• Option 2 "will come" is future tense, which is illogical for an origin that already exists.

• Option 3 "is coming" is present continuous and is used for temporary or ongoing action, not for a permanent fact.

NOTE

• Simple present is used for: universal truths, habitual actions, permanent situations, and fixed timetables.

• Verbs of state and origin such as *come from*, *belong*, *mean*, *consist of*, *contain* are normally not used in continuous tenses.

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

The term Democracy (1) ______ from the Greek (2) ______ dēmos (people) and Kratos (power). In its (3) ______ meaning, democracy means the "rule of the people". In fact it is a form of government in which all eligible people have an (4) ______ say in the decisions that affect their lives. Democracy (5) ______ a political systems existed in some Greek city-states, notably Athens following a popular uprising in 508 BC.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. words.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Dēmos" and "Kratos" are two Greek words, so the blank must be filled by the noun that names them correctly. (शब्द)

◦ Etymology is always explained as a term coming from certain words of another language.

◦ Correct: The term Democracy comes from the Greek words dēmos (people) and Kratos (power).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "letters" refers to individual characters of the alphabet (अक्षर), not to whole words like dēmos.

• Option 2 "symbols" refers to signs standing for something else (प्रतीक) and does not describe vocabulary items.

• Option 3 "numbers" refers to numerals (संख्याएँ) and is completely out of context.

NOTE

• Useful etymology one-liners: *demos* = people, *kratos* = power/rule, *archy* = rule, *cracy* = government by.

• Hence Democracy = rule of the people; Monarchy = rule by one; Oligarchy = rule by a few; Aristocracy = rule by the nobility; Autocracy = rule by one with absolute power.

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

The term Democracy (1) ______ from the Greek (2) ______ dēmos (people) and Kratos (power). In its (3) ______ meaning, democracy means the "rule of the people". In fact it is a form of government in which all eligible people have an (4) ______ say in the decisions that affect their lives. Democracy (5) ______ a political systems existed in some Greek city-states, notably Athens following a popular uprising in 508 BC.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. literal.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Literal meaning is the exact, word-for-word sense of a term, taken directly from its parts. (शाब्दिक अर्थ)

◦ Since *dēmos* = people and *kratos* = power, "rule of the people" is precisely the literal translation of the word democracy.

◦ Correct: In its literal meaning, democracy means the "rule of the people".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "metaphorical" refers to an implied comparison rather than the exact sense, so it contradicts a word-for-word translation.

• Option 2 "hyperbole" is a noun meaning deliberate exaggeration (अतिशयोक्ति); a noun cannot modify "meaning" here, and the sense is wrong.

• Option 3 "figurative" means non-literal or symbolic — the direct opposite of what the sentence requires.

NOTE

• Literal vs figurative: "He is a lion" is figurative; "A lion lives in the forest" is literal.

• Common figures of speech: Simile (as/like), Metaphor (direct comparison), Personification, Hyperbole, Oxymoron, Alliteration.

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

The term Democracy (1) ______ from the Greek (2) ______ dēmos (people) and Kratos (power). In its (3) ______ meaning, democracy means the "rule of the people". In fact it is a form of government in which all eligible people have an (4) ______ say in the decisions that affect their lives. Democracy (5) ______ a political systems existed in some Greek city-states, notably Athens following a popular uprising in 508 BC.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. equal.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Democracy is defined by the principle that all eligible citizens have the same voice in decision-making, so the positive word equal is required. (समान)

◦ The words "all eligible people" already signal inclusiveness; a negative word would contradict the definition being given.

◦ Correct: It is a form of government in which all eligible people have an equal say in the decisions that affect their lives.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "irregular" means not even or not conforming to a rule (अनियमित) and does not describe a share of power.

• Option 2 "unequal" means not the same in amount or status (असमान) — it reverses the very idea of democracy.

• Option 4 "unfair" means unjust (अनुचित) and likewise contradicts the definition.

NOTE

• Democracy phrases often tested: universal adult franchise, one person one vote, rule of law, free and fair elections.

• Abraham Lincoln's famous definition: democracy is "government of the people, by the people, for the people".

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

The term Democracy (1) ______ from the Greek (2) ______ dēmos (people) and Kratos (power). In its (3) ______ meaning, democracy means the "rule of the people". In fact it is a form of government in which all eligible people have an (4) ______ say in the decisions that affect their lives. Democracy (5) ______ a political systems existed in some Greek city-states, notably Athens following a popular uprising in 508 BC.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. as.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The preposition as is used to state the role, capacity or character in which something exists or functions. (के रूप में)

◦ Here democracy is being described in its capacity as a type of political system, so "Democracy as a political system existed…" is the correct structure.

◦ Correct: Democracy as a political system existed in some Greek city-states, notably Athens, following a popular uprising in 508 BC.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "of" shows possession or belonging and cannot link "Democracy" to its own description.

• Option 3 "over" indicates position above or authority across something and makes no sense here.

• Option 4 "in" indicates place or containment and does not express capacity or role.

NOTE

• "As" in the sense of capacity: "He works as an engineer", "She is respected as a leader", "Treat this as a warning."

• Static point: Athenian democracy, credited to the reforms of Cleisthenes in 508 BC, is regarded as the world's first known democracy.
